# Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation

###### Abstract

We propose DiffSep, a new single channel source separation method based
on score-matching of a stochastic differential equation (SDE). We craft
a tailored continuous time diffusion-mixing process starting from the
separated sources and converging to a Gaussian distribution centered on
their mixture. This formulation lets us apply the machinery of
score-based generative modelling. First, we train a neural network to
approximate the score function of the marginal probabilities or the
diffusion-mixing process. Then, we use it to solve the reverse time SDE
that progressively separates the sources starting from their mixture. We
propose a modified training strategy to handle model mismatch and source
permutation ambiguity. Experiments on the WSJ0_2mix dataset demonstrate
the potential of the method. Furthermore, the method is also suitable
for speech enhancement and shows performance competitive with prior work
on the VoiceBank-DEMAND dataset.

###### Index Terms:

source separation, stochastic differential equation, diffusion, score
matching

## 1 Introduction

Source separation (SS) refers to a family of techniques that can be used
to recover signals of interests from their mixtures. It has broad
applications, but we focus on single channel audio and speech
\[[1](#bib.bibx1)\]. This is an underdetermined problem where several
signals are recovered from a single mixture. Early success in this area
was made with methods such as non-negative matrix factorization (NMF)
\[[2](#bib.bibx2)\]. Impressive progress was brought by data-driven
methods and deep neural networks (DNN). We mention deep clustering where
a DNN is trained to create an embedding space in which the
time-frequency bins of the input spectrogram cluster by source
\[[3](#bib.bibx3)\]. Then, one can recover isolated sources by creating
masks corresponding to clusters of bins and multiply the spectrogram
with it. These methods then evolved to networks predicting mask values
directly \[[4](#bib.bibx4)\]. All these data-driven methods require to
solve the fundamental source permutation ambiguity. Namely, there is no
inherent preferred order for the sources. This is usually handled by
permutation invariant training (PIT) \[[5](#bib.bibx5)\]. In PIT, the
objective function is computed for all permutations of the sources and
the one with minimum value is chosen to compute the gradient. Recently
very strong time-domain baselines such as Conv-TasNet
\[[6](#bib.bibx6)\] or dual-path transformer \[[7](#bib.bibx7)\] have
been proposed. We mention also all-attention based \[[8](#bib.bibx8)\],
multi-scale networks \[[9](#bib.bibx9)\], WaveSplit
\[[10](#bib.bibx10)\], and the recent state-of-the-art TF-GridNet
\[[11](#bib.bibx11)\] back in the time-frequency domain. For a survey
and benchmarks of recent methods see \[[12](#bib.bibx12),
[11](#bib.bibx11)\]. All these recent approaches are trained with a
discriminative objective such as the scale-invariant
signal-to-distortion ratio (SI-SDR) \[[13](#bib.bibx13)\]. Except the
traditional methods, such as NMF, few approaches leverage generative
models. One exception adversarially trains speaker-specific generative
models and uses them for separation \[[14](#bib.bibx14)\].

Unlike discriminative methods, generative modelling allows to
approximate complex data distributions \[[15](#bib.bibx15)\]. Recently,
score-based generative modelling (SGM) \[[16](#bib.bibx16)\], also known
as diffusion-based modelling, has made rapid and impressive progress, in
particular in the domain of image generation \[[17](#bib.bibx17)\]. SGM
defines a forward process that progressively transforms a sample of the
target distribution into Gaussian noise. Given its score-function, i.e.,
the gradient of the log-probability, the target distribution can be
sampled by running a reverse process starting from noise. Crucially, the
score-function is (usually) unknown, but can be approximated by a DNN
using a simple training strategy \[[18](#bib.bibx18)\]. Recent
approaches result from the combination of score-matching and Langevin
sampling \[[16](#bib.bibx16), [19](#bib.bibx19), [20](#bib.bibx20)\].
Two frameworks have been proposed to unify various approaches, one based
on graphical models \[[21](#bib.bibx21)\], and the other on stochastic
differential equations (SDE) \[[22](#bib.bibx22)\]. SGM has quickly
found application in audio and speech processing. It has been
successfully applied in speech synthesis \[[23](#bib.bibx23),
[24](#bib.bibx24), [25](#bib.bibx25), [26](#bib.bibx26)\], speech
restoration \[[27](#bib.bibx27), [28](#bib.bibx28)\], and bandwidth
extension \[[29](#bib.bibx29)\]. Surprisingly, perhaps, several SGMs
have been proposed for speech enhancement, a typically discriminative
task \[[30](#bib.bibx30), [31](#bib.bibx31), [32](#bib.bibx32),
[33](#bib.bibx33)\]. Besides sound, but perhaps closest to this work,
separation of images using deep generative priors and Langevin sampling
has been demonstrated \[[34](#bib.bibx34)\]. However, to the best of our
knowledge, a diffusion-based speech separation method has yet to be
proposed.

We fill this gap by proposing what we believe is the first
diffusion-based approach for the separation of speech signals. The
proposed algorithm, DiffSep, is based on a carefully designed SDE that
starts from the separated signals and converges in average to their
mixture. Then, by solving the corresponding reverse-time SDE, it is
possible to recover the individual sources from their mixture. See Fig.
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")
for an illustration. We propose a modified training strategy for the
score-matching network that addresses ambiguity in the assignment of the
sources at the beginning of the inference process. We demonstrate the
method on the widely used WSJ0_2mix benchmark dataset
\[[3](#bib.bibx3)\]. While it does not outperform, yet, discriminative
baselines in terms of separation metrics, it achieves high non-intrusive
DNSMOS P.835 \[[35](#bib.bibx35)\] score, indicating naturalness. In
addition, our approach is also suitable for speech enhancement by
considering the noise as just an extra source, and performs comparably
to prior work \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\] on the VoiceBank-DEMAND dataset
\[[36](#bib.bibx36)\].

## 2 Background

### 2.1 Notation and Signal Model

Vectors and matrices are represented by bold lower and upper case
letters, respectively. The norm of vector $`\boldsymbol{x}`$ is written
$`\|\boldsymbol{x}\|=(\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x})^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}`$.
The $`N\times N`$ identity matrix is denoted by $`\boldsymbol{I}_{N}`$.

We represent audio signals with $`N`$ samples by real valued vectors
from $`\mathbb{R}^{N}`$. We introduce a simple mixture model with $`K`$
sources,

|     |                                                                   |     |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{y}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}\boldsymbol{s}_{k},`$ |     | (1) |

where $`\boldsymbol{s}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}`$ for all $`k`$. We remark
that this model can account for environmental noise, reverberation, and
other degradation by adding an extra source. By concatenating all the
source signals, we obtain vectors in $`\mathbb{R}^{KN}`$. We define in
this notation the vector of separated sources and their average value,

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                  |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{s}=[\boldsymbol{s}_{1}^{\top},\ldots,\boldsymbol{s}_{K}^{\top}]^{\top},\quad\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}=K^{-1}[\boldsymbol{y}^{\top},\ldots,\boldsymbol{y}^{\top}]^{\top}.`$ |     | (2) |

We can define the time-invariant mixing operation as a multiplication by
$`(\boldsymbol{A}\otimes\boldsymbol{I}_{N})`$ where $`\boldsymbol{A}`$
is a $`K\times K`$ matrix, and $`\otimes`$ is the Kronecker product.
Multiplying a vector $`\boldsymbol{v}\in\mathbb{R}^{KN}`$ by such a
matrix amounts to multiplying by $`\boldsymbol{A}`$ all sub-vectors of
length $`K`$ with elements taken from $`\boldsymbol{v}`$ at interval
$`N`$, i.e.,

|                            |                                                                                                                                                                             |     |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- |
|                            | $`\displaystyle\left((\boldsymbol{A}\otimes\boldsymbol{I}_{N})\boldsymbol{v}\right)_{kN+n}=\sum*{\ell=1}^{K}A*{k\ell}\,v\_{\ell N+n},\quad\begin{array}[]{l}k=1,\ldots,K,\\ |
| n=1,\ldots,N.\end{array}`$ |                                                                                                                                                                             |

To lighten the notation, we overload the regular matrix product as
$`\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{v}\triangleq(\boldsymbol{A}\otimes\boldsymbol{I}_{N})\boldsymbol{v}`$
in the rest of this paper. Next, we define the projection matrices

|     |                                                                                                                                |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{P}=K^{-1}\mathds{1}\mathds{1}^{\top},\quad\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}=\boldsymbol{I}_{K}-\boldsymbol{P}.`$ |     | (5) |

where $`\mathds{1}`$ is the all one vector, of size $`K`$ here. The
matrix $`\boldsymbol{P}`$ projects onto the subspace of average values,
and $`\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}`$ its orthogonal complement. For example, a
compact alternative to
([1](#S2.E1 "In 2.1 Notation and Signal Model ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
is $`\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{s}=\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}`$.

### 2.2 SDE for Score-based Generative Modelling

Score-based generative modelling (SGM) via SDE is a principled approach
to model complex data distributions \[[22](#bib.bibx22)\]. First, a
diffusion process starting from samples from the target distribution and
converging to a Gaussian distribution can be described by the following
stochastic differential equation

|     |                                                                                             |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle d\boldsymbol{x}_{t}=f(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t)\,dt+g(t)\,d\boldsymbol{w}_{t}`$ |     | (6) |

where $`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\,:\,\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}`$ is a
vector-valued function of the time $`t\in\mathbb{R}`$,
$`d\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$ is its derivative with respect to $`t`$, and
$`dt`$ an infinitesimal time step. Functions
$`f\,:\,\mathbb{R}^{N}\to\mathbb{R}^{N}`$ and
$`g\,:\,\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}`$ are called the drift and diffusion
coefficients of $`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$. The term $`d\boldsymbol{w}_{t}`$
is a standard Wiener process. For more details on SDEs, see
\[[37](#bib.bibx37)\]. We insist that the time $`t`$ in the diffusion
process is unrelated to the time of the audio signals that will appear
later in this paper.

A remarkable property of
([6](#S2.E6 "In 2.2 SDE for Score-based Generative Modelling ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
is that under some mild conditions, there exists a corresponding
reverse-time SDE,

|     |                                                                                                                                                                     |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle d\boldsymbol{x}_{t}=-[f(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t)-g(t)^{2}\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}\log p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t})]\,dt+g(t)\,d\bar{\boldsymbol{w}},`$ |     | (7) |

going from $`t=T`$ to $`t=0`$ \[[38](#bib.bibx38)\]. Here,
$`d\bar{\boldsymbol{w}}`$ is a reverse Brownian process, and
$`p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})`$ is the marginal distribution of
$`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$.

During the forward process, $`\boldsymbol{x}_{0}`$ being known, it is
usually possible to have a closed-form formula for
$`p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})`$. For an affine $`f(\boldsymbol{x},t)`$, it is
Gaussian and its parameters, i.e., mean and covariance matrix, usually
tractable \[[37](#bib.bibx37)\]. However, in the reverse process,
$`p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})`$ is unknown, and thus
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 SDE for Score-based Generative Modelling ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
cannot be solved directly. The key idea of SGM \[[16](#bib.bibx16),
[19](#bib.bibx19), [22](#bib.bibx22)\] is to train a neural network
$`\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x},t)`$ so that
$`\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x},t)\approx\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\log p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})`$.
Provided that the approximation is good enough, we can generate samples
from the distribution of $`\boldsymbol{x}_{0}`$ by numerically solving
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 SDE for Score-based Generative Modelling ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")),
replacing $`\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\log p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})`$ by
$`\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x},t)`$.

### 2.3 Related Work in Diffusion-based Speech Processing

SGM first found widespread adoption for the generation of very high
quality synthetic images, e.g. \[[17](#bib.bibx17)\]. Speech synthesis
is thus a logical candidate for its adoption \[[23](#bib.bibx23),
[24](#bib.bibx24)\]. In this area, several approaches that shape the
noise adaptively for the target speech have been proposed. One uses the
local signal energy \[[25](#bib.bibx25)\], while the other introduces
correlation in the noise according to the target spectrogram
\[[26](#bib.bibx26)\]. Bandwidth extension and restoration also require
to generate missing parts of the audio and high quality diffusion-based
approaches have been proposed \[[29](#bib.bibx29), [27](#bib.bibx27),
[28](#bib.bibx28)\]. Diffuse \[[30](#bib.bibx30)\] and CDiffuse
\[[31](#bib.bibx31)\] use conditional probabilistic diffusion to enhance
a noisy speech signal. Also for speech enhancement, Richter et al. have
proposed another approach \[[32](#bib.bibx32), [33](#bib.bibx33)\] based
on solving the reverse-time SDE corresponding to the forward model

|     |                                                                                                                                                   |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle d\boldsymbol{x}_{t}=\gamma(\boldsymbol{y}-\boldsymbol{x}_{t})\,dt+g(t)\,d\boldsymbol{w},\quad\boldsymbol{x}_{0}=\boldsymbol{s}.`$ |     | (8) |

This is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE that, in the forward direction, takes
the clean speech $`\boldsymbol{s}`$ progressively towards the noisy one
$`\boldsymbol{y}`$.

## 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

![Refer to
caption](2210.17327v2/paper_reverse_diffusion_example_000.png)

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Illustration of the diffusion-mixing process. From left to
right, the sources start separated and progressively mix as more and
more noise is added. The reverse process starts from the mixture and
ends with separated sources. The spectrograms were produced by actual
separation of the mixture on the right using the proposed method.

We propose a framework for applying SGM to the source separation
problem. Essentially, we design a forward SDE where both diffusion and
mixing across sources happen over time. Each step of the process can be
described as adding an infinitesimal amount of noise and doing an
infinitesimal amount of mixing. This can be formalized as the following
SDE

|     |                                       |                                                                                                                                 |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle d\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\gamma\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}\boldsymbol{x}_{t}\,dt+g(t)d\boldsymbol{w},\quad\boldsymbol{x}_{0}=\boldsymbol{s},`$ |     | (9) |

where $`\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}`$ is defined in
([5](#S2.E5 "In 2.1 Notation and Signal Model ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
and $`\boldsymbol{s}`$ in
([2](#S2.E2 "In 2.1 Notation and Signal Model ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")).
We use the diffusion coefficient of the Variance Exploding SDE of Song
et al. \[[22](#bib.bibx22)\],

|     |                                                                                                                                                       |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle g(t)=\sigma_{\min}\left(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}\right)^{t}\sqrt{2\log\left(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}\right)}.`$ |     | (10) |

The SDE
([9](#S3.E9 "In 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
has the interesting property that the mean of the marginal
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}`$ goes from the vector of separated signals at
$`t=0`$ to the mixture vector $`\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}`$ as $`t`$ grows
large. This is formalized in the following theorem proved in Appendix
[6](#S6 "6 Appendix: Proof of Theorem ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation").

###### Theorem 1.

The marginal distribution of $`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$ is Gaussian with
mean and covariance matrix

|     |                                          |                                                                                     |     |      |
| --- | ---------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}`$    | $`\displaystyle=(1-e^{-\gamma t})\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}+e^{-\gamma t}\boldsymbol{s}`$ |     | (11) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\lambda_{1}(t)\boldsymbol{P}+\lambda_{2}(t)\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}`$   |     | (12) |

where if we let $`\xi_{1}=0`$, $`\xi_{2}=\gamma`$, and
$`\rho=\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{\sigma_{\min}}`$, then,

|     |                                 |                                                                                                            |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\lambda_{k}(t)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\sigma_{\min}^{2}\left(\rho^{2t}-e^{-2\xi_{k}t}\right)\log\rho}{\xi_{k}+\log\rho}.`$ |     | (13) |

Fig.
[1](#S3.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")
shows an example of the process on a real mixture. We now have an
explicit expression for a sample $`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$,

|     |                                                                                                                                                                   |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{x}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}+\boldsymbol{L}_{t}\boldsymbol{z},\quad\boldsymbol{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{I}_{KN}),`$ |     | (14) |

where
$`\boldsymbol{L}_{t}=\lambda_{1}(t)^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}\boldsymbol{P}+\lambda_{2}(t)^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{2}}}\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}`$.
Fig.
[2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")
shows the evolution of some of the parameters of the distribution of
$`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$ over time. We can make the difference of
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{T}`$ and $`\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}`$ arbitrarily small
by tuning the value of $`\gamma`$. In addition, we observe that the
correlation of the noise added onto both sources increases over time due
to the mixing process.

Previous work on speech enhancement has successfully applied the
diffusion process in the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) domain with
a non-linear transform \[[33](#bib.bibx33), [32](#bib.bibx32)\]. The
approach we propose could be equally applied in the time-domain or in
any linearly transformed domain such as the STFT. However, since the
process of
([9](#S3.E9 "In 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
models the linear mixing of the sources, we cannot apply a non-linear
transformation. Instead, we perform the diffusion process in the
time-domain, but operate our network in the non-linear STFT domain of
\[[33](#bib.bibx33)\], as described in Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Model ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation").

Figure 2: Evolution of some of the parameters of the SDE
([9](#S3.E9 "In 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
over time.

### 3.1 Inference

At inference time, the separation is done by solving
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 SDE for Score-based Generative Modelling ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
with the help of a score-matching network
$`\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x},t,\boldsymbol{y})\approx\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}}\log p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x})`$.
The initial value of the process is sampled from the distribution,

|     |                                                                                                                            |     |      |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_{T}\sim\mathcal{N}(\bar{\boldsymbol{s}},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{T}\boldsymbol{I}_{KN}).`$ |     | (15) |

Then, we adopt the predictor-corrector approach described in
\[[22](#bib.bibx22)\] to solve
([7](#S2.E7 "In 2.2 SDE for Score-based Generative Modelling ‣ 2 Background ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")).
The prediction step is done by reverse diffuse sampling. The correction
is done by annealed Langevin sampling \[[20](#bib.bibx20)\].

### 3.2 Permutation and Mismatch-aware Training Procedure

To train the score network
$`\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x},t,\boldsymbol{y})`$,
we propose a slightly modified score-matching procedure. But, first, we
follow the usual procedure. Thanks to Theorem
[1](#S3.EGx11 "Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"),
the score function has a closed form expression. The computation is
similar to that in \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\], and we obtain

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                       |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}\log p(\boldsymbol{x}_{t})=-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}^{-1}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t})=-\boldsymbol{L}_{t}^{-1}\boldsymbol{z}.`$ |     | (16) |

The training loss is

|     |                              |                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |      |
| --- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{z},t}\left\|\boldsymbol{q}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t,\boldsymbol{y})+\boldsymbol{L}_{t}^{-1}\boldsymbol{z}\right\|_{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}}^{2}`$ |     | (17) |
|     |                              | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{z},t}\left\|\boldsymbol{L}_{t}\boldsymbol{q}_{\theta}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t,\boldsymbol{y})+\boldsymbol{z}\right\|^{2},`$                               |     | (18) |

where
$`\boldsymbol{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(\boldsymbol{0},\boldsymbol{I}_{KN})`$,
$`t\sim\mathcal{U}(t_{\epsilon},T)`$, and $`\boldsymbol{x}_{0}`$ is
chosen at random from the dataset. We use the norm induced by
$`\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}`$ which is equivalent to the weighting scheme
proposed by Song et al. \[[16](#bib.bibx16)\]. This scheme makes the
order of magnitude of the cost independent of
$`\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}`$ and lets us avoid the computation of the
inverse of $`\boldsymbol{L}_{t}`$.

However, when training only with the procedure just described, we found
poor performance at inference time. We identified two problems. First,
there is a discrepancy between
$`\mathbb{E}[\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_{T}]=\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}`$ from
([15](#S3.E15 "In 3.1 Inference ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
and $`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{T}`$. While $`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{T}`$ contains
slightly different ratios of the sources in its components,
$`\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}`$ does not. Second, the network needs to decide
in which order to output the sources. This is usually solved with a PIT
objective \[[5](#bib.bibx5)\]. To solve these challenges, we propose to
train the network in a way that includes the model mismatch.

For each sample, with probability $`1-p_{T}`$, $`p_{T}\in[0,1]`$, we
apply the regular score-matching procedure minimizing
([18](#S3.E18 "In 3.2 Permutation and Mismatch-aware Training Procedure ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")).
With probability $`p_{T}`$, we set $`t=T`$ and minimize the following
alternative loss,

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{T}=\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{x}_{0},\boldsymbol{z}}\min_{\pi\in\mathcal{P}}\left\|\boldsymbol{L}_{T}\boldsymbol{q}_{\theta}(\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_{T},T,\boldsymbol{y})+\boldsymbol{z}+\boldsymbol{L}_{T}^{-1}(\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{T}(\pi))\right\|^{2},`$ |     |

where $`\bar{\boldsymbol{x}}_{T}`$ is sampled from
([15](#S3.E15 "In 3.1 Inference ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")),
$`\mathcal{P}`$ is the set of permutations of the sources, and
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{T}(\pi)`$ is $`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{T}`$ computed for
the permutation $`\pi`$. The rational for this objective is that the
score network will learn to remove both the noise and the model
mismatch. We note that for speech enhancement, there is no ambiguity in
the order of sources and the minimization over permutations can be
removed.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Datasets

We use the WSJ0_2mix dataset \[[3](#bib.bibx3)\] for the speech
separation experiment. It contains 20000 ($`30\text{\,}\mathrm{h}`$),
5000 ($`10\text{\,}\mathrm{h}`$), and 3000 ($`5\text{\,}\mathrm{h}`$)
two speakers mixtures whose individual speech samples were taken from
the WSJ0 dataset. The utterances are fully overlapped and speakers do
not overlap between training and test datasets. The relative
signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the mixtures is from
$`-5\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}5\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}`$. The sampling frequency
is $`8\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}`$. In addition, we use the clean test set of
Libri2Mix \[[39](#bib.bibx39)\] to test mismatched conditions.

For the speech enhancement task, we use the VoiceBank-DEMAND dataset
\[[36](#bib.bibx36)\]. It is a collection of clean speech samples of 30
speakers from the VoiceBank corpus degraded by noise, recorded as well
as artificial. The dataset is split into train
($`8.6\text{\,}\mathrm{h}`$), validation ($`0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{h}`$),
and test ($`0.6\text{\,}\mathrm{h}`$). The SNR of the mixtures ranges
from $`0\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}15\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}`$ for training and
validation, and from $`2.5\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}17.5\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}`$
for testing. The sampling rate of the mixtures is
$`16\text{\,}\mathrm{kHz}`$.

### 4.2 Model

We use the noise conditioned score-matching network (NCSN++) of Song et
al. \[[22](#bib.bibx22)\]. An STFT and its inverse layer sandwich the
network and, in addition, we apply the non-linear $`c(x)`$ transform
proposed in \[[33](#bib.bibx33)\] after the STFT, and its inverse before
the iSTFT,

|     |                                 |     |                                              |
| --- | ------------------------------- | --- | -------------------------------------------- | --- | ------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle c(x)=\beta^{-1} | x   | ^{\alpha}e^{j\angle x},\quad c^{-1}(x)=\beta | x   | ^{\nicefrac{{1}}{{\alpha}}}e^{j\angle x}.`$ |     | (19) |

The real and imaginary parts are concatenated. The network has $`K+1`$
inputs, one for each of the target sources plus one for the mixture on
which we condition, and $`K`$ outputs.

### 4.3 Hyperparameters for Inference and Training

For inference, we use 30 prediction steps. For each one, we do one
correction step with step size $`r=0.5`$. The networks are trained using
Pytorch with the Adam optimizer. We use exponential averaging of the
network weights as in \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\].

Separation We use $`\gamma=2`$, $`\sigma_{\min}=0.05`$,
$`\sigma_{\max}=0.5`$. For the transformation
([19](#S4.E19 "In 4.2 Model ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")),
we use $`\alpha=0.5`$ and $`\beta=0.15`$. The probability of selecting a
sample for modified training is $`p_{T}=0.1`$. The effective batch size
is 48 and the learning rate $`0.0005`$. We trained for 1000 epochs and
we chose the one with largest SI-SDR on a sentinel validation batch.

Enhancement The SDE parameters are $`\gamma=2`$, $`\sigma_{\min}=0.05`$,
$`\sigma_{\max}=0.5`$. The transformation
([19](#S4.E19 "In 4.2 Model ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation"))
uses $`\alpha=0.5`$ and $`\beta=0.15`$. We found it beneficial to use
PriorGrad \[[25](#bib.bibx25)\] for the noise generation. The variance
of the process noise for a given sample is chosen as the average power
of the 500 closest samples in the mixture. In the enhancement setting,
there is no permutation ambiguity so we always order the sources with
speech first and noise second. We use $`p_{T}=0.03`$. The effective
batch size was 16 and the learning rate 0.0001. The network was trained
for around 160 epochs.

![Refer to caption](2210.17327v2/paper_samples_annotated_2.png)

Figure 3: Spectrograms of the clean sources (bottom row) and the
separated speech obtained by applying the proposed method to their
mixture (top row). The three samples, from left to right, were chosen
randomly from the bottom $`10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$, mid
$`80\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$, and top $`10\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ samples
sorted by SI-SDR. The SI-SDR of the samples is indicated at the top. In
the low quality sample, the spectrogram looks good, but we can see block
permutations of the sources occurring.

### 4.4 Results

We measure the performance in terms of SI-SDR \[[13](#bib.bibx13)\],
perceptual evaluation of speech quality (PESQ) \[[40](#bib.bibx40)\],
extended short-time objective intelligibility (ESTOI)
\[[41](#bib.bibx41)\], and the overall (OVRL) metric of the deep noise
challenge mean opinion score (DNSMOS) P.835 \[[35](#bib.bibx35)\].

| Dataset      | Model                           | SI-SDR | PESQ | ESTOI | OVRL |
| ------------ | ------------------------------- | ------ | ---- | ----- | ---- |
| WSJ0_2mix    | Conv-TasNet \[[6](#bib.bibx6)\] | 16.0   | 3.29 | 0.91  | 3.21 |
| (matched)    | DiffSep (proposed)              | 14.3   | 3.14 | 0.90  | 3.29 |
| Libri2Mix    | Conv-TasNet \[[6](#bib.bibx6)\] | 10.3   | 2.60 | 0.80  | 2.95 |
| (mismatched) | DiffSep (proposed)              | 9.6    | 2.58 | 0.78  | 3.12 |

|                                                 |        |      |       |      |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------ | ---- | ----- | ---- |
| Model                                           | SI-SDR | PESQ | ESTOI | OVRL |
| Conv-TasNet \[[6](#bib.bibx6)\]                 | 18.3   | 2.88 | 0.86  | 3.20 |
| CDiffuse^(†) \[[31](#bib.bibx31)\]              | 12.6   | 2.46 | 0.79  | —    |
| SGMSE+^(†) \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\]                | 17.3   | 2.93 | 0.87  | —    |
| DiffSep (proposed)                              | 17.5   | 2.56 | 0.84  | 3.09 |
| ^(†) results reported in \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\]. |        |      |       |      |

Table 2: Enhancement results on the VoiceBank-DEMAND dataset.

Separation Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.4 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")
shows the results of the speech separation experiments. We also train a
baseline Conv-TasNet \[[6](#bib.bibx6)\] network. On the intrusive
metrics, SI-SDR, PESQ, and STOI, the proposed method scores lower than
the baseline. However, it scores higher on the non-intrusive OVRL
metric. Informal listening tests further reveal that low separation
metrics are often due to very natural sounding permutations of the
speakers. This problem seems to happen for similar sounding speakers.
Example spectrograms of poor, fair, and high quality separation results
are shown in Fig.
[3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 4.3 Hyperparameters for Inference and Training ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation").

It was reported that diffusion-based enhancement performs well in
mismatched condition \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\]. We thus evaluated the model
trained on WSJ0_2mix on the Libri2Mix \[[39](#bib.bibx39)\] clean test
set. The proposed method still scores lower than Conv-TasNet for SI-SDR,
PESQ, and STOI, but the metric degradation is smaller, e.g.
$`1\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}`$ less reduction of SI-SDR. On the other hand,
the proposed method still enjoys fairly high OVRL score, indicating good
perceptual quality.

Enhancement Table
[2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")
shows the results of the evaluation of the noisy speech enhancement
task. The proposed method performs very similarly to other diffusion
methods CDiffuse \[[31](#bib.bibx31)\] and SGMSE+ \[[32](#bib.bibx32)\].
We obtain an SI-SDR higher by $`0.2\text{\,}\mathrm{dB}`$, but PESQ
value closer to that of CDiffuse. ESTOI is somewhere in the middle. The
OVRL metric suggests good perceptual quality, but was not provided for
the other methods. In terms of SI-SDR particularly, a gap remains with
discriminative methods such as Conv-TasNet.

## 5 Conclusion

We proposed DiffSep, the first speech source separation method based on
diffusion process. We successfully separated speech sources, and
demonstrated that our approach extends to noisy speech enhancement. For
separation, there was a substantial gap in performance with
state-of-the-art discriminative methods. We believe this may be due to
both outputs being from the same distribution, thus confusing the
generative model. We have done initial work to alleviate the permutation
ambiguity, using a modified training strategy for the score-matching
network, but further work is likely necessary to robustify the inference
procedure against permutation mistakes. Bringing in proven architectures
from the separation literature is an interesting area of future work. We
have also not used yet any of the theoretical properties of the
distribution of mixtures, which could be elegantly integrated in the
score network architecture, as in \[[34](#bib.bibx34)\].

## 6 Appendix: Proof of Theorem

Because the stochastic differential equation is linear,
$`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$ follows a Gaussian distribution
\[[38](#bib.bibx38)\]. Following Särkkä and Solin \[[37](#bib.bibx37)\],
eq. (5.50) and (5.53), the mean and covariance matrices of
$`\boldsymbol{x}_{t}`$ are the solutions of

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |      |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle d\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}=-\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t},\quad d\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}=-\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}-\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}\widehat{\boldsymbol{A}}+g(t)^{2}\boldsymbol{I},`$ |     | (20) |

respectively, with the initial conditions
$`\boldsymbol{\mu}_{0}=\boldsymbol{x}_{0}`$ and
$`\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{0}=\boldsymbol{0}`$. The solution for
$`d\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}`$ is given by the the matrix exponential
operator,

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |      |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{t}=e^{-\gamma t\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}}\boldsymbol{x}_{0}=exp(0)\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{x}_{0}+exp(-\gamma t)(\boldsymbol{I}-\boldsymbol{P})\boldsymbol{x}_{0}.`$ |     | (21) |

Substituting $`\boldsymbol{x}_{0}=\boldsymbol{s}`$,
$`\boldsymbol{P}\boldsymbol{x}_{0}=\bar{\boldsymbol{s}}`$, and
rearranging terms yields
([11](#S3.E11 "In Theorem 1. ‣ 3 Diffusion-based Source Separation ‣ Diffusion-based Generative Speech Source Separation")).
For $`\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{t}`$, we work in the eigenbasis of
$`\gamma\bar{\boldsymbol{P}}`$ and solve differential equations with
respect to its distinct eigenvalues, $`0`$ and $`\gamma`$. $`\square`$
